title: Surfaces As A Classification Problem
notes: Open by making the classification theorem feel computational instead of mysterious. The source chapter supplies the theorem flow, but the lecture will keep returning to three inspectable ledgers: polygon words for construction, orientation constraints for global consistency, and Euler or surgery bookkeeping for normal form.

title: Closed Surfaces Supply Finite Data
notes: Stress the local-to-global tension. Every point of a closed surface has a planar neighborhood, so local pictures look the same, but the global surface may still carry handles or crosscaps. The deck uses quotient polygons and triangulations because they turn that global information into finite data.

title: Classification Ledger
notes: Use the notebook ledger as the first invariant dashboard. The orientable family is indexed by handle number, the nonorientable family by crosscap number, and the sphere sits as the shared starting point. Point out immediately that the mixed case is normalized once a crosscap appears.

title: Euler Characteristic Is Necessary But Not Complete
notes: This is the warning slide for overusing one number. The torus and Klein bottle both have Euler characteristic zero, so chi cannot be the entire classification. The same issue reappears at chi equals minus two, where H(2) and M(4) still require the orientability bit.

title: Surface Symbols Are Quotient Instructions
notes: Treat the polygon word as a recipe rather than a decorative boundary label. Walking around the boundary records labels and directions; gluing equal labels according to arrows builds the surface. The figure lets students check that the raw edge data is finite and auditable.

title: Polygon Symbol Proof Roadmap
notes: Give a compact roadmap without pretending to run the full reduction algorithm on the slide. The important teaching move is that edge labels must pair, standard orientable symbols pair opposite directions, and reduction moves preserve the quotient surface while simplifying the word toward normal form.

title: Orientability As A Sign Constraint
notes: Translate orientability into a graph propagation problem. Assign one triangle an orientation, let each shared edge force the neighbor sign, and continue through the dual graph. Success means a coherent global choice exists; a contradiction records the combinatorial trace of a one-sided loop.

title: The First Contradiction Is The Evidence
notes: Use the check table to connect the diagram to actual notebook data. The sphere and torus propagate orientations consistently, while the Klein bottle model reaches incompatible sign requirements on a shared edge. The point is not the particular edge numbers, but the existence of a forced contradiction.

title: Euler Characteristic Uses A Primal Tree And Dual Graph
notes: Frame Armstrong's Euler argument as a two-graph ledger. A maximal tree in the one-skeleton contributes chi equal to one, and the complementary dual graph accounts for the remaining cells. The notebook artifact makes this dependency visible instead of leaving the proof as only algebra.

title: Euler Proof Roadmap
notes: Walk slowly through the proof compression. A connected graph has Euler characteristic at most one, so chi of the surface is chi of the maximal tree plus chi of the dual graph, hence at most two. Equality forces the dual graph to be a tree, matching the sphere case in the proof strategy.

title: Surgery Raises Chi Toward The Sphere
notes: Present surgery as controlled simplification. Cutting a two-sided nonseparating curve removes a cylinder and adds two disks, raising chi by two. Cutting a one-sided curve removes a Mobius band and adds one disk, raising chi by one. Each move reduces complexity while tracking orientability.

title: Connected Sum Reverses The Bookkeeping
notes: Connected sum is the reverse construction language for the same classification ledger. Removing one disk from each surface loses two Euler units before gluing boundaries, so the formula chi(S # T) equals chi(S) plus chi(T) minus two. The mixed example explains why a handle plus a crosscap becomes three crosscaps.

title: Surgery Euler Lab
notes: Use the embedded lab as an instructor dashboard rather than as a proof substitute. The H(3) path climbs by two under two-sided surgeries until it reaches the sphere. The M(5) path climbs by one under one-sided surgeries, and orientability returns only at the final sphere.

title: Normal Form Algorithm
notes: This slide turns the classification theorem into a short decision procedure. If there are no crosscaps, the surface remains orientable and the number of handles is the genus. If any crosscap is present, each handle converts to two crosscaps and the surface is recorded as M(2m+n).

title: Classification Ledger Proof Roadmap
notes: Now assemble the separate ledgers. Polygon symbols provide construction data, orientability decides which family can contain the surface, Euler characteristic determines the parameter in that family, and surgery explains why every closed connected surface reaches a standard form. This is the theorem as an instructor-ready workflow.

title: Recap: Three Ledgers Must Agree
notes: Close by asking students to triangulate any claim through the three ledgers. The word ledger says how the surface is assembled, the orientation ledger says whether local orientation survives globally, and the Euler or surgery ledger says where the surface sits in the classification table. Agreement is the real evidence.
